stem: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of Amazon Bedrock's pricing model for on-demand usage?

options.text: A flat annual license fee with unlimited usage
Pay-as-you-go billing based on the number of input and output tokens processed
Billing based solely on the number of AWS accounts used
No billing of any kind for any usage

explanation.why_correct: Bedrock's default on-demand pricing model bills pay-as-you-go based on the number of input and output tokens processed, which is the defining characteristic of this pricing tier.

why_incorrect.A: Bedrock does not use a flat annual license fee for on-demand usage; it uses token-based billing.
why_incorrect.C: Billing is not based on account count; it scales with actual token usage.
why_incorrect.D: Bedrock usage is billed; it is not free of any charges.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Amazon Bedrock's default pricing model is on-demand, pay-as-you-go, billed per input token and per output token processed.

stem: A company wants to distinguish which Amazon Q product to use for a scenario involving reviewing pull requests and suggesting code fixes. Which product fits?

options.text: Amazon Q Business
Amazon Q in Connect
Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Q in AWS Supply Chain

explanation.why_correct: Reviewing pull requests and suggesting code fixes is a coding-assistance task, exactly matching Amazon Q Developer's purpose as the coding assistant.

why_incorrect.A: Amazon Q Business is the enterprise knowledge assistant, not a coding-review tool.
why_incorrect.B: Amazon Q in Connect assists contact-center agents; it is unrelated to code review.
why_incorrect.D: Amazon Q in AWS Supply Chain focuses on supply chain insights; it is unrelated to code review.

stem: Which AWS storage service most commonly serves as the source document location for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion?

options.text: Amazon S3
Amazon EC2 instance store
AWS Snowball
Amazon Route 53

explanation.why_correct: Amazon S3 is the commonly used source document location for Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion, serving as the storage layer from which documents are chunked and embedded.

why_incorrect.B: EC2 instance store is ephemeral local storage tied to a specific instance; it is not the standard source for Knowledge Bases ingestion.
why_incorrect.C: AWS Snowball is a physical data transfer device for bulk migrations; it is not the ongoing source location for Knowledge Bases.
why_incorrect.D: Amazon Route 53 is a DNS service; it has no relevance to document storage for Knowledge Bases.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Source documents commonly live in Amazon S3 for Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion.

stem: Which statement correctly describes RDS for PostgreSQL's role as a vector store option on AWS?

options.text: It supports the pgvector extension, enabling storage and querying of embeddings using SQL.
It has no vector storage capability of any kind.
It exclusively supports graph-structured data with no relational capability.
It requires abandoning SQL entirely to use vector features.

explanation.why_correct: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL supports the pgvector extension, letting teams store and query embeddings using familiar SQL alongside their relational data, exactly as described.

why_incorrect.B: RDS for PostgreSQL does have vector storage capability via the pgvector extension, contrary to this statement.
why_incorrect.C: RDS for PostgreSQL is fundamentally a relational database; it is not a graph-structured-data-exclusive service.
why_incorrect.D: pgvector is designed to be queried using standard SQL, not requiring SQL to be abandoned.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL supports the pgvector extension, enabling efficient storage of embeddings and similarity searches using SQL.

stem: Which of the following is a content filter category that Bedrock Guardrails can be configured to block?

options.text: Harmful content categories, such as hate speech or violence
Valid AWS billing invoices
Successfully completed API health checks
Routine CloudWatch log entries

explanation.why_correct: Bedrock Guardrails can be configured with content filters to block categories of harmful content, such as hate speech or violence, directly matching this description.

why_incorrect.B: Billing invoices are unrelated to content-safety filtering; Guardrails does not filter this kind of administrative data.
why_incorrect.C: API health checks are operational signals, not content requiring safety filtering.
why_incorrect.D: Routine log entries are operational data, not the kind of harmful content Guardrails content filters are designed to block.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Content filters block categories of harmful content as part of Bedrock Guardrails' configurable safety controls.

stem: A team wants to fine-tune a JumpStart foundation model and needs to select which SageMaker instance type will run the training job. Which capability enables this level of control?

options.text: SageMaker JumpStart's fine-tuning process, which runs within the self-managed SageMaker environment
PartyRock, since it exposes identical instance-type configuration options
Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing
Amazon Polly voice selection

explanation.why_correct: SageMaker JumpStart's fine-tuning process runs within the self-managed SageMaker environment, giving the team the ability to select specific training instance types, matching this exact control requirement.

why_incorrect.B: PartyRock is a no-code playground with no instance-type configuration exposed; it does not offer this level of infrastructure control.
why_incorrect.C: Bedrock on-demand pricing is a billing model for using existing foundation models via API; it does not expose instance-type selection for training.
why_incorrect.D: Amazon Polly voice selection is a text-to-speech configuration option, unrelated to training instance type selection.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Need full control over fine-tuning a pre-trained model's training process, including instance type selection -> SageMaker JumpStart.
